speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should in cooperation with the sugar factories encourage in every reasonable way the use of sugar made from home grown raw material.
He said: In briefly introducing this resolution, Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw to the attention of the house the conditions in a new industry, an industry that merits the attention of the members of this house and of the people of Canada on account of its great potential importance.
According to the Bureau of Statistics, in Canada we consume-I am using round figures
-971,000,000 pounds of sugar annually. Of that amount about 847,000,000 pounds are manufactured from material which is grown outside of Canada. Some 25,000,000 pounds are exported, chiefly to Newfoundland.

speechtext:
Some 50,000,000 pounds of pure sugar are imported. It can be said fairly, however, that of the amount of sugar consumed in Canada only about 10 per cent is manufactured from raw material grown in Canada. In the United States they grow the raw material for 20 per cent of the sugar which they consume, and even in Great Britain, a country with a large population and a limited agricultural area, we find that one-fifth of the sugar which they use is manufactured from material grown at home.
The relatively large importation of raw material into Canada for the making of sugar is not due to any lack of fertility in our soil. It is not because our climate is not suited to the growing of this material, because we find that in 1929 the sugar beet grown in Alberta had a larger sugar content than the beet grown in any other part of North America.
The sugar beet was originally a small root vegetable, but by cultivation, and as a result of experiments in plant breeding, the present article has been developed so that when it is grown in the sunny regions of our country it contains eighteen and even up to twenty-two per cent of sugar content.
We need have no fear about the quality of the sugar made from the sugar beet, because we find that manufacturers of sugar, with the assistance of specially skilled chemists, can produce a chemically pure product, a product that is just as pure and just as wholesome as the product of cane sugar. We find also that it conforms to the chemical formula of sugar and that it can be used for any household purpose whatsoever. Those manufacturing sugar from the cane had difficulty in removing the molasses. Those manufacturing sugar from beets had, for a time, difficulty in removing certain of the bitter acids, but these difficulties have been overcome and sugar can now be manufactured from sugar beets that will give satisfaction for every purpose.
I wish, Mr. Speaker, that my words would reach the ears of the housewives of Canada, and that I had the eloquence to persuade
Beet Sugar Industry

them to insist on using sugar manufactured from beets rather than sugar manufactured from cane, because I believe that if they would do that they would be doing a great patriotic sendee to a struggling industry in this country. If we used more beet sugar we would, of course, import less of the cane sugar, and it would be interesting to see how this would affect our trade and commerce. We are told that if we are going to sell to other countries we must buy from them, that exports must be paid for by imports. It is interesting to note from what countries we get nine-tenths of the sugar that we use. In 1930, we imported sugar, in the usual classification not above No. 16 of the Dutch standard, as follows:

From those countries we imported that great quantity of raw material for the manufacture of sugar. At this particular time there is a very good reason why the people of Canada should use sugar made from Canadian material. That urgency consists in the saving of the many irrigation projects that are now on the verge of ruin. In Alberta alone provision has been made to place a million acres of land under irrigation, and about half that amount is actually under irrigation at the present time. During the last thirty years millions of dollars have been spent on irrigation schemes. Some of this money was secured from the provincial governments, some from the transportation companies and some from the long-suffering British investors. Those investors and the men who actually carried out the earth-moving developments hoped for profits. On the other hand however they must be credited with vision. They had a picture of those dried'-out areas being turned into fertile gardens capable of producing bountiful crops to feed our great population. They had a vision of neatly painted cottages housing a contented people. They felt they were making a contribution towards the building of empire, and money was not spared for supervision, for colonization schemes, for demonstration plots and things of that nature. Years have passed and their hopes have not

been realized. Investors and operators alike have ibeem deplorably disappointed by the limited success and the many disasters encountered in connection with these irrigation projects. The land cost the settlers some $50 to $70 per acre; the water cost $1.50 per acre, or $2 per acre per season. Owing to the collapse in prices of farm produce in the last few years Wheat-growing is a dead loss. The farmers cannot grow fodder crops to feed live stock because the price of stock has depreciated accordingly. The irrigation farmer must work long hours during the day and often long hours of the night in the mud and water to look after his fields, and he has come to the place where he finds that in spite of his original investment, and in spite of the years of hard work, he has no equity in the land, he does not own his home and has no hope for the future.
In reviewing the situation, may I say it seems clear that part of the failure in these irrigation districts is due to the fact that they have not been able to grow crops of a high acre value. In the western states beet-growing is the very basis and foundation of irrigation farming. In the state of Montana which, in area, is somewhat similar to that of Alberta, we find that they have 55,000 acres under beets whereas we in Alberta have only about
12,000	We find that they have three sugar factories and we have only one. Growing a crop such as sugar 'beets would to a great extent save the irrigation farmers and, to at least some degree reclaim or regain some of the investments Which outside interests have made. Sugar beets would provide a cash crop for irrigation farmers. The present price of $5.50 per ton is too low to allow a profit, and too low to make feasible the beginning of operations by new factories. True, the growers receive a bonus on aocount of high sugar content, and if they grow ten tons per acre, which is a usual crop, they receive a cash price of from S60 to $65 per acre. Then, again, the growing of sugar beets would constitute a great link in crop rotation and would help to make possible the proper balancing of farm operations. Growing this crop would provide a system of cultivation which would help to keep down the weeds, wild oats and all foreign growth, and would increase by 50 per cent the productivity of other crops, such as alfalfa and sweet clover, which would be grown in rotation with the sugar beets.
Perhaps the most important effect of the growing of sugar beets would be the advantages derived from the by-products such as the beet pulp, beet tops, molasses and so on.

Beet Sugar Industry
The production of these by-products would encourage the live stock industry, the development of secondary industries, and would necessitate the use of, and demand for, fuel, lumber and lime. Work would be provided for thousands of Canadians, our railroads would reap some benefit, and undoubtedly the stabilization and development of the farming industry, to a very great exent, would be the result. I have tried to show that we need have no fears about the quality of sugar we can produce from our beets, that preparation has been made to grow large quantities of sugar beets, that we have a market in Canada for nine times as much of this product as we are growing at the present time, and that great advantages would accrue to people in the irrigated districts if the sugar market could 'be secured.
At this point I wish briefly to mention some of the ways this government could assist the industry. I realize fully that immediate assistance must be given because the people on those farms are about discouraged and cannot longer continue under their present system of farming. The collapse in prices during the past few years has brought them to that condition. I do not think the question of tariffs enter largely into the matter. Canada has entered into a treaty with the West Indies in which the duty on sugar has been definitely stated and, for that reason, it is not likely that tariffs could be used to relieve the present situation. However, there are other methods which could be used to assist this 'industry., Loans might be made to responsible individuals sufficient to give them an opportunity to start a factory and thus create a market for the farmers in the immediate district. This government has on other occasions loaned money for various purposes. I may point out that in the district of which I am speaking the farm loan board has practically excluded the local farmers from the benefit of the act, so probably assistance along the lines which I have indicated would in a measure compensate them for that exclusion. It may be said at once: Why not let joint stock companies be formed and have them apply to the government for the assistance required? We must remember that those who have capital are extremely cautious these days and will not enter into a new business enterprise unless they know there is a reasonable chance of success.
Another method of assistance is by subsidy. I find in Great Britain this industry is so encouraged. Under the British Sugar Beet Subsidy Act, passed in 1924, a subsidy is granted to home-grown beet sugar for ten
years, at the rate of 19 shillings and 6 pence per hundredweight for the first four years, 13 shillings per hundredweight for the next three years, and 6 shillings and 6 pence per hundredweight for the remaining three years. In 1924, the number of sugar beet growers was 4,039, and the total acreage 22,637. Six years later, in 1930, the number of growers had increased to 40,415, and the acreage to 348,920; that is, the growers had increased tenfold in number, the acreage fifteenfold. It is interesting to find that the factories had increased from three to eighteen, the labour employed from 1,435 to 9,900 persons. It is significant, too, that Great Britain has captured the confectionery trade of a large part of the world.
Now, Mr. Speaker, for excellent reasons this government gave a bonus of 5 cents per bushel to the growers of wheat. This assistance, I may say, was much appreciated, and I believe if the government could see its way clear to grant a bonus of $1 or $1.50 per ton to the growers of sugar beets they would bring hope and encouragement to many homes in the irrigated districts. Those people who are now on the verge of despair would be encouraged by such a move.
There is one other method I might suggest by which the government could help and encourage the growers of sugar beets and promote the development of this industry. That is by a system of advertising. It is not a new form of assistance. We have spent money on advertising to encourage the use of Canadian hemp, and the consumption of Canadian grapes and Canadian apples.	It
would seem to me, therefore, that some of the money that has been voted to the Department of Trade and Commerce for advertising purposes might well be used to encourage our people to use sugar made from the raw materials grown right within our country. Whatever methods may be adopted to this end, I hope they will be sufficient and effective; and I also hope that they will be applied immediately, because the very low price of farm products during the last year or two has made this a very urgent and a very important question.
The great national value of a sugar beet factory as compared with a cane sugar refinery can be easily shown by roughly contrasting the two operations. Cane sugar is grown in tropical countries and imported as a raw product, to be melted, filtered and purified in the refineries. On the other hand, Canadian labour is required in the production of beet sugar, and it starts from the seeding -in fact it starts before the seeding, because the land must be prepared; then we go
4S8
Beet Sugar Industry

through all the processes of seeding, weeding, thinning and cultivating the crop during the growing season, followed by the harvesting operations and the transportation of the crop to the factory. Much Canadian labour is required for all these operations. At the factory the beets must be sliced and steeped and the resultant juice dealt with. In fact 60 per cent of the factory investment is used before the beet sugar reaches the stage at which the refinery first gets the cane sugar, so that twice as many men, twice as much fuel, and double the quantity of supplies are required in the production of beet sugar.
Beet sugar factories are needed in the irrigated district at Brooks and Vauxhall, and probably at Medicine Hat and Lethbridge, or wherever they can be most economically operated. In many cases local capital is not available, but if some assistance could be given along the lines I have suggested I believe more factories would be established, and thus a great service would be done to those Canadians who have invested their all and devoted years of their lives to the growing of sugar beets, only to find themselves now in a very unfortunate position.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, with all deference, if the government can see its way clear to give some assistance to this industry, that it be given in such a way that it will reach the sugar beet growers, because they are the ones who most need assistance and encouragement. By so doing I believe the government would, in a limited way, help to solve the unemployment problem, which is the greatest problem confronting the dominion at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, in supporting the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw), let me say that Canada has been known as a country suited to agriculture. Many agricultural products have been produced of late, however, for which the farmer cannot find a market, though agriculture in this country is still the primary industry, from the point of view not only of the number of persons engaged in it, but also of the capital invested. I believe I am safe in saying that at the present time agriculture is in distress, and that when agriculture is in distress practically the whole country is in distress.

As everyone knows, sugar is a staple product. According to the returns issued by the Bureau of Statistics, last year our importations of sugar were valued at about $21,000,000. In many parts of Canada to-day we have farmers who cannot find a market for their products, but here is an article which, if manufactured in Canada, would provide a market for at least one product of the soil and would give encouragement to the agricultural industry which is badly needed at the present time.
In British Columbia we have the Fraser valley, which is admirably adapted to the growing of sugar beets. Two or three years ago a United States concern came into the Fraser valley and encouraged the farmers to grow beets, which were shipped to the state of Washington and manufactured into sugar. If we are to depend upon a concern which is not within the control of this country, the growing of sugar beets will not be encouraged at all, and I think it should be fostered on this side of the line. The growing of sugar beets and the manufacture of sugar should be encouraged by the province of British Columbia; it would not only provide a market for a product of the soil but would also provide work for a great many people who to-day are seeking employment.
We import sugar, but there is another product of the sugar beet of which up to the present we have imported a great deal. I refer to beet pulp, which is used in the dairying industry. If we could grow enough sugar beets and establish factories in British Columbia I think a good market could be developed for that product also. I believe this resolution merits the attention of every hon. member of this house, especially those who represent agricultural constituencies. So I have great pleasure, Mr. Speaker, in seconding the resolution.

Mr. Speaker, it is with considerable diffidence that I rise to speak to this resolution, because the mover has so clearly placed before the house the facts with regard to the use of sugar throughout Canada. In fact I find myself limited in my remarks to rather a parochial statement, in that I must confine myself to the constituency I represent, which is very much interested in the growing of sugar beets and also in the other subject dealt with by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw), that of irrigation.
I appreciated the very clear manner in which the hon. member placed before the house the needs of the people in southern Alberta, and I should like to endorse many

Beet Sugar Industry
of his statements. The growing of sugar beets in western Canada, especially in southern Alberta, is not possible except in connection with irrigated lands. Therefore irrigation and sugar beets go hand in hand; they are interlocked, and they are questions which must be decided in conjunction with each other.
I should like to digress for a few moments and speak of irrigation, because in a large measure agriculture in southern Alberta cannot be carried on without irrigation, at least as far as the semi-arid region is concerned. In a large part of that area there is an average annual rainfall of from 13 to 16 inches, and this must be supplemented by irrigation if crops are to be raised. The Rocky mountains to the west supply us with great quantities of water, enabling the irriga-tionist on the prairie to produce his crops, but even without this irrigation I should tell the house that with a normal rainfall these semiarid regions have produced many millions of bushels of the very finest wheat in the world. But, owing to the fact that for a number of years in succession we have had a very limited rainfall, the question of irrigation has been brought very much to the fore, and as a result I think in that respect we have expanded and gone ahead far too rapidly and to a much greater extent than we should have.
As the hon. member for Medicine Hat said, the total irrigated acreage of southern Alberta is over one million acres, of which hardly one-half is under cultivation. Of course, the most extensively irrigated areas in Canada are to be found in southern Alberta; other irrigated areas such as the fruit areas in British Columbia and the ranching areas in southeastern Saskatchewan are very small in comparison, and I venture to say that few members of this house and very few people who reside in Alberta have any idea of the size of the irrigated areas in that province and the vast amount of capital invested. The records show that in Alberta we have four corporations that have installed works for irrigation; we have seven irrigation districts and 332 privately owned schemes. Of the four corporate projects, three are under the control of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and I should like to tell the house the size of those districts and the area that can be irrigated in each. The Canadian Pacific Railway area at Lethbridge gets its water from the St. Mary river, and contains
99,000	acres. The Canadian Pacific Railway west area contains 300,000 acres, the eastern area 400.000 acres and the area supplied by the Canada Land and Irrigation
Company 130,000 acres. Then there are the irrigation districts, the Taber, with 21,661 acres, the Lethbridge northern with 100 000 the New West with 4,501, the Little Bow with 3,090, the Magrath with 6,975, the Raymond with 15,129, and the United with 34,235. In all, with the 332-privately owned schemes, we have 1,090,806
acres available.	. ,
Many of these irrigation works were carried on with money raised through the sale of bonds issued by the various districts, and in some cases those bonds were endorsed by the Alberta government. The people who resided in the districts were not able to meet the annual interest charges, and as a result the districts have been taken over by the provincial government and to-day are being operated under government supervision. The money tied up in these irrigation districts amounts to a tremendous sum. When I say that the initial investment in the province of Alberta is over 835,000,000 and that we have spent many millions more in betterment and upkeep, the house will realize just what liability the people of this country have in these irrigation schemes. It is true we have a great asset in these irrigable lands, and this asset runs far beyond the canal that carries the water or the ditches that bring it to the several farms. I also want to point out that there are very few of us who realize the immense liabilities that face those who have to meet the bonded indebtedness thereon. If we are to avoid any danger in regard to the security that is invested, the people who live on these lands must be enabled to grow specialized crops which will bring more in return than the ordinary wheat farmer could get if he were to put all of his land under wheat. These irrigated lands are adapted to the growing of specialized crops that cannot be produced on dry land, and the mistake that the irrigation farmer has made in the past has been that he has confined his efforts to a single crop that would bring in the most return with the least effort, and that is wheat. The last returns we have from the irrigation projects show that in the year 1928-that was the last return we were able to get-more than 66 per cent of the land under irrigation was devoted to wheat. That is a great mistake. The years that have followed have shown that we must find some other crop to supplement that wheat crop. The farmers have recognized that and they are now going in for specialized crops.
Among specialized crops I might mention alfalfa, because we can produce annually from four to five tons per acre of luscious alfalfa
Beet Sugar Industry

hay from these irrigated lands; and we can also raise alfalfa seed, for in 1931 we took first and second prizes at the Chicago and Toronto fairs for alfalfa seed grown east of Calgary. The first prize for potatoes was captured by a farmer living in the immediate vicinity of Lethbridge; and so far as the sugar beet is concerned I shall show what has been produced within the last year, and what that country is capable of producing in that direction. When we come to specialized crops there are two points to be taken into consideration-first of all agricultural suitability, and secondly the economic value that can be obtained from the growth and harvesting of the crop. As regards agricultural suitability, as the hon. member for Medicine Hat has pointed out, there is no crop that is more suitable for irrigated areas than sugar beets; and so far as economic value is concerned, it is still the best crop, because we find that there is a greater return from its production than from any other crop grown on these lands in the west. And the large acreage that is kept under sugar beet production in the western states, where they have conditions similar to our own, goes to prove that this is the best-paying crop to be found on the North American continent, so far as irrigation is concerned.
I will not go on to tell the house anything about the agricultural suitability of the sugar beet as a crop for the irrigation farmer, but I would place before the house some facts with regard to two farmers living on one of these irrigation tracts, side by side, one on a northwest and the other on the northeast quarter sections north of Lethbridge. The first farmer had this last year 33 acres of sugar beet, which produced 330 tons, giving a return of SI,715; 12 acres of alfalfa, 48 tons, S384; 30 acres of wheat, from land which the previous year had grown sugar beets and from which he secured 46 bushels per acre, giving a return of $438; 24 acres of wheat following wheat, 25 bushels per acre, with a return of S210; 20 acres of oats following wheat, the return being $270 ; 8 acres of barley following wheat, giving $96, making a total of $3,113, from a farm of 160 acres. Besides this he had 28 acres of sweet clover for pasture purposes. This man keeps from eight to ten milch cows besides pigs, chickens and ducks, and he has a wonderful garden producing all kinds of vegetables. He had an income of over $3,000. Now listen to what his neighbour had. He was a wheat farmer, leaving some of his land for fallowing in the summer; he would alternate, putting in half his land this year and the other half next year. 
He had 100 acres of wheat and he received $700. Compare the two: One man with an income of $3,113 and the other with $700.
The sugar beet crop has meant very much to the farmers in the irrigated areas of southern Alberta during the past year. Seven hundred farmers in 1931 on 12,000 acres of sugar beet land produced 105,000 tons and received from the company $630,000. In other words, those 700 farmers received an average of $900 each; or, for each acre they had under cultivation, they received $52.50. The highest previous yield was in 1927 when the farmers produced 7.72 tons per acre. This year, through better cultivation and a wiser use of fertilizer, which we find practically at our doors, being able to secure it from the Consolidated Smelters of Trail, we have increased the tonnage to 8.75 tons per acre, which is an increase of over one ton per acre. We have around Lethbridge what is known as the 15 Ton Beet Club. Membership in this club is limited to those who have grown sugar beets and have produced more than 15 tons per acre on a 5 acre plot. This year we find that the gentleman who secured first prize produced 21.797 tons per acre on his 5 acres, receiving $595 cash; the second prize went to the farmer who produced 19-36 tons per acre, receiving $480 for his plot; the third prize to the farmer who produced 17-641 tons per acre, receiving $440; and the fourth prize to the farmer who produced 17-227, for which he got $430.
The money spent in connection with these sugar beets is vast, and it goes to a great number of people. The sugar company paid $630,000 to these farmers who raised the sugar beets; but these farmers in turn had to pay in wages to the 1,500 men who hoed the crop, the sum of $250,000. That was what was paid out in labour. And coming to the expenses in connection with running the factory, we find that last year the sugar factory paid 335 men $165,000. Their supplies were:

This makes a total of $665,500 for factory labour, supplies and freight. The grand total distributed through that one sugar plant in the immediate vicinity of Lethbridge was therefore, in the last year, SI,295,500. The year before it was over $1,400,000. The result has been of great benefit to those who grow sugar beets. I am informed by an official of one of the irrigation companies that 80 per cent of the beet growers paid all or part of their irrigation rates during 1931, whereas only 40 per cent of the non-beet growers paid any rates at all, and that the beet growers paid back 98 per cent of the loans they had secured in 1931 from the credit societies, whereas only 40 per cent of the non-beet growers paid back any of those loans.
The manager of the beet factory, in speaking at a meeting a few days ago, had this to say:
The beet growers here had received $5.50 per ton for last year's beets due to the high sugar content in spite of the low prices of sugar. Mr. Wood here stated that the beets grown in this factory district last year were the best beets grown on the American continent, being the highest in sugar content.
Therefore I can endorse the statement made by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw), but I should like to elaborate further on it. The sugar content of the beets grown in southern Alberta this year was as high as 18.34 per cent; that of beets grown in the United States was 17 per cent, and that of beets grown in Great Britain was 15 per cent, so that in all probability the sugar beets raised in southern Alberta have the highest sugar content of any beets grown in the world. I see an hon. member from Quebec shaking his head. He will be at liberty, when the opportunity arises, to give his views to the house.
For some seven years we have had one sugar beet factory operating in western Canada at the town of Raymond in the constituency which I have the honour to represent. It is needless for me to inform the house that for some years previous we had a factory there, but it did not prosper very well and had to be removed to the United States. This last factory was established there in 1925 and for six years operated as a straight beet sugar concern. But last April, or to be accurate, on April 23, 1931, this sugar beet factory was purchased by the Cane Sugar Refineries of British Columbia, and it is now operated as part of their plant. This sugar beet concern, having been placed with the cane sugar interests, is hardly seeking expansion. I think the management are not very anxious to expand. But the sugar beet growers of
southern Alberta are most anxious that we shall have another factory and they are asking for an expansion. The present management limited the sugar beet acreage from 14,000 to
12,000	acres last year, and it may be they will be able to take a few more acres next year because I believe they are about to spend some $300,000 in betterments in their factory.
So far as this question is concerned, I have from the very first avoided interjecting politics into it. It is too large a question to permit of the introduction of politics; it means too much to the people of southern Alberta and also to that very much greater question, irrigation in southern Alberta. But when one finds some officials of a local beet growers' association, who have always taken a great interest in politics, and quite rightly so, using their official position to advance the interests of the Liberal party, either on their own account or by guidance or assistance from the heads of the party in the city of Lethbridge, and seeming to be more anxious to advance the interests of the Liberal party than to secure an expansion of the industry, I think the time has arrived when the member who represents that constituency should stand in his place and inform the house as to the particular situation of this industry. Last session the hon. member for Medicine Hat quite rightly questioned the government regarding their attitude as to assisting the industry. I sat silent, thinking it would be in the best interests of the community that they should hear the definite reply from the minister in charge, the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) who was then Minister of Finance. But when politicians who belong to the beet growers and officials of some of the local organizations take an opportunity to publish certain statements in a paper that is not friendly to the government, that is not friendly to the gentleman who leads the party, a gentleman of whom I am extremely proud and to whom I hope to be most loyal, it makes me feel it is time for me to explain some of the details regarding this matter. In that paper they state they are disappointed at and dissatisfied with the attitude of the present government as regards expansion of the sugar beet industry. The first statement which, in all courtesy, I should like to make to hon. members opposite is that if in southern Alberta we have only one sugar beet factory instead of two, it is due to the tariff policy of our hon. friends opposite and to the lack of assistance and support by the former administration to this industry when it was in its infancy. I informed the house that this industry operated for six years as a straight

sugar beet factory. It could have been assisted by the then Liberal government as a straight sugar beet cooperative association, but things were allowed to continue until the project had almost reached the point where it could not operate any longer. They applied for assistance, but all the assistance they got was permission to bring in second-hand machinery free. The former administration gave no assistance except that they allowed this company to bring in secondhand machinery free. The instability of Canadian tariff policy as affecting sugar has been the factor which very largely has prevented progress in the establishment of a domestic sugar beet industry.

The irrigation project in which my hon. friend is now so much interested was launched at a time when I happened to be premier of the province; I was premier when the bonds were guaranteed, consequently I had a good deal of interest in the constituency and in the project to which my hon. friend has referred.

May I say to my hon. friend from Lethbridge however, and to this house, that so far as the industries in this country are concerned, my position is only too well known. I never encouraged an industry to come into Canada by any promise that it would be bonused or helped-never on any occasion. My hon. friend will not be traducing my position if he states that I held out any hope that if that industry came to Canada I would at

It is quite possible that if sugar had been at its present price that industry would not have been established in Lethbridge. The fact is, however, that sugar prices were then higher; the prices of farm produce were higher, and I was perfectly correct, from the information I possessed, in my statement in this house that the company did intend to expand.

The sugar industry started in Canada nearly fifty years ago with bounties from the Dominion government. It was developed in Ontario by the Ontario Agricultural college. It was subsidized to the extent of half a cent a pound in this province, until to-day we have a type of sugar beet which contains more than double the sugar content of the beets grown at the inception of the industry. In my part of the country thousands of people depend on the sugar beet industry; the growing of sugar beets gives a tremendous amount of work to the farmers, and the conveyance of the crop to the factories is a source of income not only to the trucking concerns but also to the manufacturers and distributors of trucks. The land for the growing of sugar beets is either irrigated, as in the west, or, as in our part of the country, land which has been improved by very expensive drainage.
For a number of years in my county we were able to send sugar beets into the United States, and quite a large industry was developed along that line; to-day our sugar beets can no longer be exported to that market. As a result of this and other causes the curtailment of sugar beet growing in my part of the country is a real hardship on those engaged in the industry. The farmers have prepared their land for this crop and it is highly taxed, they have secured the machinery necessary for their farming operations, and the trucks for hauling their crops to the factories, and any measure which will in any way not only ensure a continuance of the beet growing industry but also increase the acreage under cultivation would certainly be of real value to our fanners.
I have a great deal of pleasure in supporting the amendment to the resolution, because I believe that if this whole matter is thoroughly threshed out before the agriculture committee much information will be elicited that will be of service to the farmers and others, even including my good friend from West Edmonton. The amendment proposes that the committee study the question of helping the beet sugar industry by way of customs duty, bonus or otherwise. I would suggest that under the "otherwise" the question of quotas be studied. This system may be new in Canada, but it is frequently discussed in Europe. In a study of the quota system made at the last Imperial conference it was particularly stressed that articles to be usefully treated under the system must go through some one definite avenue of distribution. Surely the sugar industry of Canada presents a bottle neck that would very well lend itself to at least a study of the 
question of establishing a quota for beet sugar grown in Canada. I am told that in France and in Italy from time to time they definitely set the quota of home-grown wheat which must enter into their domestic flour production. When the committee meets I hope they will consider the question whether it would be possible to establish a quota for Canadian grown sugar that our sugar interests would be forced to apply in the sugar they produce and distribute throughout the dominion. The quota possibly could be based at the beginning on the average acreage over a period of five years, to be gradually increased year by year until the percentage of home grown sugar to the imported had reached a certain level. I am not sure whether this is possible, but I think it is worth while studying. It may appeal to our friends on the other side inasmuch as its adoption would not be raising the customs duties. It has the further value that despite the fact that the sugar industry of Canada may be in the hands of a very few persons, they will be forced gradually to increase the number of acres under cultivation and so assure for the farmers of Canada a fair distribution of their own production throughout the dominion. With that addition to the amendment I have much pleasure in supporting the resolution.

I have consulted a very interesting book published in Ottawa by Mr. J. B. Spencer, The Maple Sugar Industry in Canada. In this work a careful study is made of the progress of the maple sugar industry in Canada. With the indulgence of the house I should like to quote rather extensively from it. The writer says:
The making of maple sugar, which is confined entirely to the American continent, had a very early beginning, as before the advent of the white man, the Indian had learned to extract and concentrate the sap of the maple tree. On the approach of spring, the trees were gashed with a tomahawk, in a slanting direction, and beneath the opening was inserted a wooden chip or spout to direct the fluid, drop by drop, into receptacle resting on the ground. The sap was caught in a birch bark dish and boiled in earthen kettles. The small quantity of dark, thick syrup thus made was the only sugar available to the Indians, and is stated by early writers to have been highly prized. The first settlers learned from the Indians the art of maple sugar making and followed for perhaps a century their crude methods of manufacture, except for the substitution of iron or copper kettles for vessels of clay or bark. In the early days, before the timber acquired much value, the axe continued to be used for tapping the trees, and the sap was caught in wooden troughs and conveyed in buckets to a central point to be boiled. The boiling was done in large iron kettles suspended from a pole in the open woods, in a sheltered location but with no protection from the sun, rain, snow or the ashes, falling leaves, moss and bits or bark that were driven about by the wind. The products made by this crude method were strong in flavour, dark in colour and variable in quality. In the past 50 years, however, maple sugar making has become a rather highly organized commercial industry. An early improvement was the substitution of the auger for the axe in tapping, coopered buckets taking the place of the birch bark "caso" or hewn sap trough, while the kettle gave way to the evaporating pan which has in late years developed into the modern evaporator with corrugated bottom and separate compartments. Not alone for the conservation of the life of the tree but also for cleanliness in sugar making, the wooden spout has almost disappeared in the most advanced sections; in fact, the present tendency is toward the use of metal in every article of equipment with which the sap, syrup or sugar comes in contact.

To answer that question I quote from a letter dated April 29, 1931, from the Bow Valley Sugar Beet Association:
The purchase by the B.C. people of the Raymond factory is a severe blow to our hopes and I, personally, am not for one moment deceived by their intentions, as announced in the press, of continuing to operate the factory at Raymond.
The secretary of tihe Bow Valley Sugar Beet Association, under date of April 29, 1931, wrote the Prime Minister of Canada as follows:
I am convinced that the purchasers will close the Raymond factory at the earliest possible moment and on the slightest of pretext and that the purchase was put through for the purpose of killing competition from the beet sugar factory at Raymond.
I have no hesitation in saying that the
sugar combine, of which the British Columbia refineries are a part, will destroy all other separate industries which may be created either on a bonus or on any other basis. That is not the way to deal with the problem.
Now I come to the producers' point of view. The same gentleman, the secretary of the Bow Valley Sugar Beet Association, wrote from Bassano on May 16, 1931, as follows:
I enclose herewith sample crop share contract used by the growers and tenants on the Raymond project in 1929, from which you will gather that the total cost per acre, divided as therein set out, amounted to $54.30 on an average yield of eight tons to the acre, which was about the average, and at $7 to the ton the average farmer just about broke even.
And no more. At S7 a ton they broke even, and no more. Since that letter was written however the factory has reduced its price to the farmers from $7 or $7.50 to $5.50 per ton. I have no hesitation in saying that since that time the average beet grower has not made money, and has been very lucky if he broke even. Undoubtedly there have been one or two outstanding illustrations where some money has been made. In almost every industry or occupation in Canada there could be found one or two growers who, through fortunate circumstances, climatic or soil conditions, made a profit. The propounders of bonus policies always pick those few out as striking illustrations. They do not however represent the true state of affairs. The representative from Lethbridge who addressed the sugar beet association of Strathmore, was a gentleman named Robertson whom possibly my hon. friend from Lethbridge may know. Mr. Robertson is alleged to be a practical man who has carried on farming operations in southern Alberta for sixteen years, and last year successfully harvested 75 acres of sugar beets. What did he tell that meeting? Did he give them hope or enthusiasm? Listen to what he says:
.... in 1930, 14,000 acres in the Raymond area produced 128,000 tons, distributing to the farmers over $800,000. . . .
Those figures indicate that there was a production of $} tons to the acre, which was worth about $800,000 to the farmers. Of course that sounds very splendid in the aggregate. In answer to a question he said:
Costs would run from $45 to $50 per acre.
There is the statement of a practical farmer engaged in the production of sugar beets who says that costs will run from $45 to $50 per acre, and the farmer receives only about $55 when it is marketed. There would not seem to be much hope there.
Beet Sugar Industry

There is one further point I wish to impress upon hon. members, namely that the growing of sugar beets is a peculiarly difficult farm operation. The quality of the beet depends upon large quantities of water in the month of September to promote proper pollenization because the beet receives most of the sugar content in that month. For that reason sugar beets cannot be grown in western Canada, except under irrigation, so that water m'ay be put on at proper times. That is probably one reason why costs are so high in the production of sugar beets. The labour entailed throughout the year in their production is of such a character that the average Canadian or American will not participate in it. The result is that during the last several years in the province of Alberta growers have imported oriental and central European labourers to attend to their crops.

Mr. Speaker, before a vote is taken on this motion, as a representative from the maritimes, I wish to make a few observations. As the hon. member who moved the resolution is one of the most genial and likable members in the house I am sure it is not easy for hon. members on this side to oppose anything he would wish to introduce, especially when it would benefit the people of his own constituency. The argument he put forward is largely that it would help out the irrigation system and possibly give a return to the men who have invested their money in the sugar beet industry.
As has been pointed out by the member for West Elgin (Mr. Hepburn), the largest sugar production perhaps in the history of the world is in sight at the present time, and the difficulty for the sugar producing countries is to find a market for their product. There was a time in the maritime provinces when Cuban sugar was imported, and in exchange we were able to send large quantities of our potatoes and other agricultural products. Under the present practice of applying dumping duties we find sugar is being shut out of almost every market in the world. Cuban sugar has been excluded from our market. Naturally the Cuban government have practically refused to accept any of our maritime province products. As you know, Mr. Speaker, last year a representative from this government was sent down to Cuba to see if an arrangement could be made to find a market for our potatoes. The Cuban paper Mundo carried the following item:
Commercial relations between Cuba and Canada, after expiration of the existing modus vivendi in December, were discussed at a conference between Canadian minister Macdonald, Canadian commercial attache Marmaek, officials of the Departments of State, and of Agriculture, Commerce and Labour, and members of the tariff commission. The state department is said to have indicated that Cuba will not change her tariff policy, but will consider modifications in favour of Canada provided that country makes special concessions as to Cuban sugar, rum and tobacco, and the Canadian representatives agreed to study the question.
If the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ryckman) were in his seat I would ask him to tell the house whether, as has been asserted several times this afternoon, and as I have good reason to believe, the dumping duty has been applied in a good many cases. I would also ask if any effort has been made by the government to find a market in Cuba or in other parts of the world for our potatoes, and especially if they have endeavoured to raise the British embargo. We hear our friends

Charges by Hon. G. N. Gordon
from the west talking about the desperate straits of the farmers in the prairie provinces.
I doubt if any farmers are in a more desperate condition than the farmers in the maritime provinces who have been engaged in the production of potatoes on a large scale.

Not at all. To-day the
farmers of Prince Edward Island have millions of bushels of potatoes on their hands, for which they cannot get over 8 or 10 cents a bushel at the very most; the farmers of New Brunswick are in an even worse position, having to sell their crop at 20 to 25 cents a barrel; Quebec is in a similar position.
The Cuban government put before our representative a definite proposition; they asked him if the Canadian government was willing to consider some arrangement whereby a treaty could be worked out. Mr. Macdonald replied:	I will present these facts to
my government, and they will take them under consideration.
The time has arrived when, if we are going to bonus one branch of industry, we have got to bonus every branch, else we must stop this bonusing system. You cannot bring in discriminatory measures such as are being advocated in this house in favour of one branch of industry and leave other farmers to shift for themselves. You cannot build up their industry and make them prosperous by means of bonuses. Everyone knows the system has failed; it has failed across the line, it has failed in Canada. The only thing we have to do is to face the situation and endeavour to get our products into all the countries of the world, and so give our farmers a chance to compete on fair and equal terms. I believe the time has come when we in Prince Edward Island might very well ask that the local starch industry be bonused. Our farmers are compelled to turn their potatoes over to the starch factory at 5 or 6 cents a bushel delivered; they practically have to give them away. How in the world can farmers exist under such conditions? If any body of men in Canada should ask for a bonus after two or three years of the conditions I have described it is the farmers of the maritime provinces.
I am sorry to be compelled to oppose the resolution and also to vote against the amendment.
